01.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were eating a meal together, with Rav Aḥa, son of Rava, serving them. Ameimar said the blessing over wine before every cup, Mar Zutra only over the first cup and the cup after Grace after Meals, and Rav Ashi only over the first cup. When Rav Aḥa asked whose practice to follow, Ameimar said he had kept changing his mind about drinking more; Mar Zutra said he followed the students of Rav; Rav Ashi said the law is not like the students of Rav, pointing to Rav's own ruling on the order of blessings when a Festival falls after Shabbat.
01.why: Rava has just defended saying a second blessing on the cup after Grace by citing the students of Rav, who held that preparing to say Grace ends one's intention to drink. The three Sages here split over that very principle; the Gemara then rejects Rav Ashi's proof.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: One of three Sages at the meal; he blessed every cup because each time he had meant it to be his last.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Dined with Ameimar and Rav Ashi; he followed the students of Rav and blessed the first and last cups.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The third Sage at the meal; he blessed only the first cup and argued the law is not like the students of Rav.

people.name: Rav Aḥa, son of Rava
people.about: Served the three Sages at the meal and asked them whose practice to follow.

terms.meaning: The blessings said after eating a meal with bread, often recited over a cup of wine.
The blessing that sanctifies Shabbat or a Festival at its start, said over wine.
The blessing at the end of Shabbat or a Festival that marks the separation between holy time and ordinary time.
Jewish law; the practical ruling that is followed.

02.note: Rabbi Akiva once picked the fruit of an etrog tree on the first day of the month of Shevat. He set aside two different tithes from it: one as if the new year for trees had already begun, following Beit Shammai, and one as if it had not, following Beit Hillel.
02.why: The mishna gives the first of Shevat as the new year for trees according to Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel say the fifteenth. Rabbi Akiva's double tithe shows him unwilling to decide between them; Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda then says his doubt was really between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and, unsure which year it belonged to, set aside two tithes from it.

terms.meaning: A citron, a lemon-like fruit; its tree has some rules of a tree and some of a vegetable.
A tenth of produce set aside for a religious purpose. Which tithe is due depends on the year of a seven-year cycle: second tithe in some years, poor man's tithe in others.
The schools of two early Sages, Shammai and Hillel, who disagree on many points of law.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

03.note: In the forty years before the Second Temple was destroyed, the signs of favor stopped: the lot for God never came up in the High Priest's right hand, the crimson wool strip no longer turned white, and the westernmost lamp of the candelabrum did not stay lit. The doors of the Sanctuary kept opening by themselves, until Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai scolded them: Sanctuary, why do you frighten yourself? I know you will be destroyed, as Zechariah prophesied, 'Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars.'
03.why: The Gemara has just told how, after the High Priest Shimon HaTzaddik died, the miracles of his time faded. This continues the decline down to the destruction; the Gemara then explains why the Temple is called Lebanon, the name in Zechariah's verse.

people.name: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Scolded the Sanctuary doors that opened by themselves, telling them he already knew the Temple would be destroyed.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A High Priest; during his tenure the lot for God always came up in his right hand.

terms.meaning: On Yom Kippur the High Priest drew lots to decide which of two goats was offered to God and which was sent to Azazel; the lot for God coming up in his right hand was taken as a good sign.
A red strip tied to the goat sent away to Azazel on Yom Kippur; its turning white was taken as a sign that the people's sins were forgiven.
One lamp of the Temple candelabrum that would miraculously stay lit longer than the others.
The main building of the Temple, which housed the inner holy rooms.

04.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan suffered from a disease called tzefidna and went to a gentile noblewoman known as a healer. She prepared a remedy for him on Thursday and Friday. He asked what he would do on Shabbat; she said he would not need it, and when he pressed her, she made him swear not to reveal the remedy. He swore, 'To the God of the Jews, I will not reveal it.' She told him, and he went out and taught it publicly.
04.why: The mishna cites Rabbi Matya ben Ḥarash allowing medicine to be put in the mouth of someone with throat pain on Shabbat. The Gemara then asks how Rabbi Yoḥanan could break his oath, and later explains he could treat this ailment on Shabbat because it spreads to the intestines and is dangerous.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage suffering from tzefidna who learned a healer's secret remedy under oath and then taught it publicly.

people.name: the matron
people.about: A gentile noblewoman healer who treated Rabbi Yoḥanan and made him swear not to reveal her remedy.

terms.meaning: An illness that starts in the teeth and gums, with bleeding, and moves on to the intestines.
The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, when preparing medicine is normally forbidden unless life is in danger.

05.note: Rav was reading the Torah portion aloud before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Each time a senior scholar walked in, Rabbi Ḥiyya, then bar Kappara, then Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi, he started again from the beginning. When Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama came in, Rav decided not to start over again, and Rabbi Ḥanina was offended. For thirteen years Rav went to him on the eve of Yom Kippur to ask forgiveness, and he would not be appeased. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Ḥanina had dreamt of Rav hung on a palm tree, a sign he would head a yeshiva, so he refused, so that Rav would go to study Torah in Babylonia.
05.why: The Gemara is telling stories of Sages seeking forgiveness on Yom Kippur eve. It asks how Rav could ask more than the three times Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina sets, and how Rabbi Ḥanina could refuse, given Rava's teaching that one who forgives is forgiven.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Read the Torah portion before Rabbi and, for not restarting for Rabbi Ḥanina, sought his forgiveness for thirteen years.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; the Torah portion was being read before him.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The first scholar to enter, for whom Rav restarted the reading; the translation calls him Rav's uncle and teacher.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A scholar who came in next; Rav restarted the reading for him too.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama
people.about: Was offended when Rav did not restart for him, and refused to be appeased because of a dream about Rav.

terms.meaning: The day before the Day of Atonement, when people traditionally ask forgiveness of those they have wronged.
The leader of an academy of Torah study.

06.note: Rav Dimi reported that once people forgot to bring a Torah scroll to the synagogue before Shabbat. The next day they spread sheets over posts along the way, carried the scroll to the synagogue, and read from it. The Gemara objects that they could not have spread sheets on Shabbat, since they would have had to carry them there; rather, they found sheets already spread on the posts, and brought the scroll along that path.
06.why: The Gemara has argued that neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Yosei accepts a hanging partition for carrying on Shabbat, and asks whose view the incident in Tzippori followed. This is that incident, done on the authority of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported this incident.

terms.meaning: Carrying an object through a public area is forbidden on Shabbat unless the area is enclosed by partitions that the law recognizes.
The handwritten parchment scroll of the Five Books of Moses, read in the synagogue on Shabbat.

07.note: During the water-pouring ceremony at the Temple, a Sadducee priest poured the water over his own feet instead of on the altar. In anger, all the people pelted him with their etrogim. That day a horn of the altar was damaged, and they sealed it with a lump of salt, not to make the altar fit for service but so that it would not be seen damaged.
07.why: The mishna has described the two basins for the water and wine libations, and that the one pouring water was told to raise his hand. The incident shows why; the Gemara then adds that an altar missing a horn is unfit for service, which is why the salt did not make it fit.

people.name: a Sadducee priest
people.about: Poured the water libation on his feet and was pelted by the crowd.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group of the Second Temple period that rejected many traditions of the Sages.
A ceremony on the festival of Sukkot in which water was poured out on the altar.
A citron, a lemon-like fruit held during prayers on Sukkot; the plural is etrogim.
One of the raised corners of the Temple altar.

08.note: Rav Pappi visited Mar Shmuel on a Festival and was served porridge made from crushed wheat. He did not eat it. The Gemara asks whether it might have been crushed with a small mortar and pestle, which is allowed, and answers that he saw it was too finely ground for that.
08.why: Rava has just said that crushing grain with a small mortar is permitted in Babylonia but forbidden in the Land of Israel, where people had many servants. The Gemara tests that rule against this visit, then adds that Mar Shmuel's house, which had slaves, may have been treated like the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: A guest who refused porridge served to him on a Festival.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The host at whose house Rav Pappi was served the porridge.

terms.meaning: A biblical holiday such as Passover or Sukkot, when most work is forbidden but some food preparation is allowed.
A bowl and club for pounding grain; a large one looks like ordinary weekday work and is forbidden on a Festival.

09.note: Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok recalled that he often followed his father into Rabban Gamliel's house on Festivals. Contrary to what people said, they did not sweep the dining room on the Festival: they swept it the day before and covered it with sheets, then removed the sheets when guests arrived. Nor did they burn incense on the Festival: they filled perforated iron pans with fragrant smoke the day before and plugged the holes, then opened them when guests came. The Sages answered that if so, this is permitted on Shabbat as well.
09.why: Rav Asi said the dispute over incense on a Festival is only about perfuming clothes, and burning it for the smell is allowed. This report concerns perfuming the house, so the Gemara uses it to object, and then reverses what Rav Asi is quoted as saying.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok
people.about: Recalls visiting Rabban Gamliel's house with his father on Festivals.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage whose household was said to sweep and burn incense on Festivals.

terms.meaning: An early collection of teachings that supplements the Mishna.
The dining room, where people reclined on couches to eat.
A biblical holiday on which most work is forbidden; Shabbat is stricter still.

10.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan met the young son of Reish Lakish and asked him what verse he had learned. The boy said: 'A tithe shall you tithe,' and asked what it meant. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: tithe so that you will become wealthy. Asked how he knew, he said: go and test it. The boy objected that one may not test God, and Rabbi Yoḥanan cited Rabbi Hoshaya: except here, as Malachi says, 'Bring the whole tithe... and test Me now by this.' The boy replied that had he reached that verse, he would not have needed Rabbi Yoḥanan or Hoshaya his teacher.
10.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Yoḥanan's reading of the verse: take a tithe so that you will become wealthy. This story shows a child challenging that very teaching; another story about the same boy follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Taught the boy that tithing brings wealth and defended it with a verse from Malachi.

people.name: the young son of Reish Lakish
people.about: A child who questioned Rabbi Yoḥanan sharply about the verse he had studied.

people.name: Rabbi Hoshaya
people.about: Quoted by Rabbi Yoḥanan; the boy calls him Rabbi Yoḥanan's teacher.

terms.meaning: A tenth of one's produce set aside as the Torah commands.
Demanding that God prove Himself; the Torah forbids it in Deuteronomy, 'You shall not test the Lord your God.'

11.note: Abba the Bloodletter received greetings from the heavenly academy every day, Abaye only every Friday, and Rava only on Yom Kippur eve. Abaye was upset and was told he could not do what Abba did: Abba treated men and women separately, gave women a slit garment so as not to see them exposed, and had a hidden box for fees so the poor were not shamed; he paid scholars instead of charging them. Abaye sent two Sages to test him. Abba hosted them; in the morning they took his rugs to the market. When asked to price them, he named what he had paid. He said he assumed they needed money to ransom captives, and that he had already given the rugs to charity. Rava, upset over Abaye, was told: your merit protects your whole city.
11.why: The Gemara has been telling of Sages who decreed fasts over plague. It now groups stories about the hidden merit of ordinary people; the story of the prison guard who saved women and warned the Sages follows.

people.name: Abba the Bloodletter
people.about: A bloodletter who received daily greetings from Heaven for his modesty, discretion and generosity.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage, greeted from Heaven each Shabbat eve, who sent two Sages to test Abba.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage greeted from Heaven only on Yom Kippur eve, and upset about Abaye's greater honor.

terms.meaning: The heavenly academy, imagined as a gathering of the Sages in Heaven.
An old medical treatment of drawing blood from a vein.
Paying to free captives, considered one of the most urgent forms of charity.

12.note: Rabbi Zerika told Rav Safra to see the difference between the powerful men of the Land of Israel and the pious men of Babylonia. When rain was needed, Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda in Babylonia would say: let us gather and pray, perhaps God will send rain. But Rabbi Yona, father of Rabbi Mani, would tell his household he was going to buy grain, then go out, stand in a low, hidden place covered in sackcloth, and pray, and rain would come. When he came home and was asked for the grain, he said that now that rain had come, there would be relief in the world.
12.why: The Gemara is telling stories of righteous people whose prayers brought rain, such as Abba Ḥilkiyya and Ḥanan HaNeḥba, who also hid their greatness; stories about Rabbi Yona's son follow.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: Draws the comparison between Sages of the Land of Israel and of Babylonia.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: The Sage Rabbi Zerika addresses.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: With Rav Ḥisda, one of the pious men of Babylonia who prayed for rain in public.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: With Rav Huna, one of the pious men of Babylonia who prayed for rain in public.

people.name: Rabbi Yona
people.about: Father of Rabbi Mani; he prayed for rain in secret and hid it even from his family.

terms.meaning: Rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance.
A coin.

13.note: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa, a poor man, came to own goats, especially since the Sages forbid raising small animals in the Land of Israel. Rav Pineḥas explained: a man once left chickens at his door, and his wife found them. Rabbi Ḥanina told her not to eat their eggs. The chickens multiplied until they became a nuisance, so he sold them and bought goats. Later the owner passed by and told a companion he had left his chickens there. Rabbi Ḥanina asked for an identifying sign, the man gave it, and he took the goats. These were the goats that brought home bears on their horns.
13.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's goats, accused of damaging fields, came home with bears on their horns; it now asks how he had goats at all.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
people.about: A poor and righteous Sage who kept a stranger's lost chickens and returned their worth as goats.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's wife
people.about: Found the chickens left at their door.

people.name: Rav Pineḥas
people.about: Tells how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa came to have goats.

terms.meaning: Sheep and goats, which the Sages barred from being raised in the Land of Israel because they graze in others' fields.
An identifying mark by which an owner proves that a lost item is his.

14.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decreed a fast for rain, and rain fell after sunrise. He thought to have the fast completed, but Rabbi Ami told him the rule is before noon or after noon. Shmuel HaKatan decreed a fast, and rain fell before sunrise; the people took it as praise of the community, but he said it was like a slave asking his master for a reward, and the master says: give it to him, so I do not have to hear his voice. Another time rain fell after sunset; again they took it as praise, and he said it was like a master who says: let him wait and suffer, then give it to him.
14.why: A baraita has just given three views on when rain that falls during a fast lets people stop fasting: sunrise, noon, or the ninth hour. Rabbi Ami rules by the noon view, and the Gemara then asks what Shmuel HaKatan would count as praise of the community.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Decreed a fast for rain and thought to complete it after rain fell after sunrise.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Told Rabbi Yehuda Nesia that the cutoff is noon.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: Decreed fasts for rain and twice told the people the rain was no sign of their merit.

terms.meaning: Ordered a public fast day, here to pray for rain in a drought.
A short illustrative story comparing one situation to another.

15.note: Rabbi Yirmeya, or some say Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, said that Onkelos the convert composed the Aramaic translation of the Torah from the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, and Yonatan ben Uzziel the translation of the Prophets from Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. When Yonatan made his, the Land of Israel quaked and a Divine Voice asked: Who has revealed My secrets to mankind? Yonatan stood and said: I did, not for my honor or my family's, but for Yours, so that disputes would not multiply in Israel. He wished also to translate the Writings, but the Divine Voice said: Enough. The Gemara explains: they contain the end of days, when the Messiah comes.
15.why: The Gemara has just discussed letters the prophets restored, and cites another teaching of the same Sage. It then asks how Onkelos composed the Torah translation if it already existed in Ezra's day, and why the Prophets' translation shook the land when the Torah's did not.

people.name: Yonatan ben Uzziel
people.about: Composed the Aramaic translation of the Prophets and defended it before the Divine Voice.

people.name: Onkelos the convert
people.about: Composed the Aramaic translation of the Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: The Sage who reports this, or according to others Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba.

terms.meaning: A rendering of the Bible into Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews at the time, read aloud in synagogues.
A voice from Heaven heard announcing God's will.
A Persian measure of distance, a few miles.
The third part of the Hebrew Bible, after the Torah and the Prophets, including Psalms and Daniel.

16.note: When Rav Huna died, Rav Ḥisda stopped the Sages from placing a Torah scroll on his bier, since Rav Huna had moved a scroll off his bed before sitting on it. The bier would not fit through the door, and Rav Ḥisda would not let them lower it from the roof or move him to another bier, so they broke the doorway. Rabbi Abba eulogized him. He was taken to the Land of Israel for burial beside Rabbi Ḥiyya, and Rav Ḥagga carried him into the cave. There Rabbi Ḥiyya's son Yehuda told his brother Ḥizkiyya to rise for Rav Huna; a pillar of fire rose with him, and Rav Ḥagga, frightened, stood the coffin up and left.
16.why: The Gemara is discussing the honor due a Torah scholar at his death, after Abaye told the Sages they must rend their garments for Rav Safra; Rav Ḥisda's own funeral is told next.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage whose funeral and burial in the Land of Israel are told here.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Insisted at Rav Huna's funeral on practices he had learned from Rav Huna himself.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Gave the eulogy, saying Rav Huna was worthy of the Divine Presence but for living in Babylonia.

people.name: Rav Ḥagga
people.about: Carried Rav Huna into Rabbi Ḥiyya's burial cave, citing his own purity and service to Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: With Rabbi Asi, a Sage of the Land of Israel who went out to meet Rav Huna's coffin.

terms.meaning: The frame on which a body is carried to burial.
God's presence resting on a person, here meaning the gift of prophecy.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
Tefillin: leather boxes with Torah verses, strapped to the arm and head with leather straps blackened on one side.

17.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Ḥiyya came to a town and asked to greet its Torah scholar, who was blind. Rabbi Ḥiyya urged Rabbi not to lower his dignity as Nasi and offered to go alone, but Rabbi took hold of him and went too. As they left, the blind scholar blessed them: you greeted one who is seen and does not see; may you greet the One Who sees and is not seen. Rabbi told Rabbi Ḥiyya he would have kept him from this blessing. Asked where he learned it, the scholar told of Rabbi Ya'akov of Ḥitiyya, who greeted his teacher daily and, when told in old age not to trouble himself, cited a verse: if seeing Sages at their death brings life, all the more so in their lifetime.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi, the Nasi; he insisted on visiting the blind scholar himself.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Traveled with Rabbi and offered to greet the blind scholar in his place.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov of the village of Ḥitiyya
people.about: Greeted his teacher every day; the blind scholar learned his blessing from his teaching.

terms.meaning: The president, the head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
An argument from the lesser to the greater: if something holds in a weaker case, all the more so in a stronger one.

18.note: On Ulla's journey to the Land of Israel, two men from Ḥozai joined him, and one rose and slaughtered the other. The killer asked Ulla: did I act properly? Ulla said yes, and told him to open the cut further. When Ulla came before Rabbi Yoḥanan, he asked whether he had strengthened the hands of sinners; Rabbi Yoḥanan told him he had saved his own life. Rabbi Yoḥanan wondered how such rage could happen in the Land of Israel, since the verse 'the Lord shall give you there a trembling heart' speaks of exile in Babylonia. Ulla answered that they had not yet crossed the Jordan.
18.why: The Gemara is collecting teachings about anger, beginning with Rabbi Yonatan's warning that the angry are ruled by Gehenna, built on the same verse about a trembling heart. More sayings about anger follow.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage traveling to the Land of Israel who encouraged a killer out of fear for his own life.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage in the Land of Israel who told Ulla he had acted to save himself.

terms.meaning: The Jordan River marks the eastern border of the Land of Israel; before crossing it, the travelers were still outside the land.
Encouraged wrongdoers, itself considered a sin.

19.note: Rav Ḥisda sent Rav Naḥman a question: the Sages fixed payments for kneeing, kicking and punching someone, so what is owed for a blow with a hoe? Rav Naḥman replied: Ḥisda, Ḥisda, are you collecting fines in Babylonia? Tell me what actually happened. Rav Ḥisda explained: two men shared a cistern, each drawing water on alternate days. One drew on the other's day, ignored him when told it was not his turn, and was struck with the handle of a hoe. Rav Naḥman answered that he deserved a hundred blows, since even those who forbid taking the law into one's own hands allow it to prevent a loss.
19.why: The Gemara uses this case to open a dispute: Rav Yehuda says a person may not take the law into his own hands, Rav Naḥman says he may, and all agree he may when a loss is imminent.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sent Rav Naḥman a question about payment for a blow with a hoe, then described the case.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Answered that the man struck with the hoe deserved it.

terms.meaning: A fixed penalty set by the Sages, as opposed to paying for actual loss. Babylonian courts could not impose such fines.

terms.term: taking justice into one's own hands
terms.meaning: Enforcing one's rights oneself rather than going to court.

20.note: A man cut down another man's date palm, and the two came before the Exilarch. The Exilarch said he had seen the spot himself: three palms grew there in a cluster, worth a hundred dinars together, so the man must pay thirty-three and a third. The man objected that the Exilarch judged by Persian law and took the case to Rav Naḥman, who ruled that the damage is appraised as part of an area sixty times larger.
20.why: The Gemara has just explained a baraita as teaching that damage to a field is valued as part of an area sixty times larger. Rav Naḥman applies that rule here; Rava then asks whether it applies when a person does the damage himself, as here, and not only his animal.

people.name: the Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who first judged the case and set payment at a third of the palms' value.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Judged the case again and ruled by the one-in-sixty appraisal.

terms.meaning: Valuing the damaged part as one-sixtieth of a larger plot, which yields a lower payment than valuing it alone.
A coin.
The law of the ruling Persian state, as opposed to Torah law.
